transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-18
Start: 14:00 PT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Samira Khan (Recruiter, Redwood), Ethan Brooks (Staff SE, Redwood), Elaine Wu (Candidate, Dataplane AI)

Summary: quick phone screen for senior inference engineer role. Focus: Elaine's recent work on quantization, latency profiling, and distributed KV cache strategies; culture/manager fit; basic system-design conversation. Candidate expressed interest in private deployments and edge acceleration.

Topics: role fit, recent projects, systems design for inference, deployment constraints, available start window, compensation band high-level

[00:00] Samira: Hey Elaine, thanks for taking the time. Can you hear us okay?
[00:06] Elaine: Yep, loud and clear. Thanks for setting this up.
[00:09] Samira: Quick intro — I'm Samira, recruiting partner, and Ethan is one of our senior SEs who'll do a technical pass. We'll keep it to about 40 minutes, spend 20 on background, 15 on technical, and leave room for your questions.
[00:24] Elaine: Sounds great.
[00:26] Ethan: Hi Elaine, nice to meet you. Quick note, my connection's a little spotty on the east side of the building so if I drop, I will ping.
[00:33] Elaine: Noted. No worries.

[00:35] Samira: Elaine, can you walk us through your last 3 years at Dataplane AI — what you owned and the measurable outcomes you shipped?
[00:44] Elaine: Sure. So at Dataplane, I led inference infra for their recommendation models. Primarily I was responsible for the production runtime — so deployment, autoscaling, memory optimizations. In year one I focused on quantization support; we moved ResNet-ish and custom transformer variants from fp16 to int8 with symmetric quant, and that cut GPU memory by ~38% and reduced p99 latency for shorter sequences by about 18% in our evals. The tricky bit was preserving top-k recall for recommendations, we ran a battery of A/B tests for that.
[01:24] Ethan: When you say symmetric quant, was that quant-aware training or post-training quant?
[01:29] Elaine: Mostly post-training quant with some per-channel calibration. We did a short round of fake-quant-aware fine-tuning for the top 2 layers where we saw biggest drift. That helped recover accuracy without long retraining.
[01:42] Ethan: Interesting. What library/tooling did you use?
[01:45] Elaine: Internally we used a mix — started with ONNX quantization flow, but we ended up writing a light wrapper because our custom ops didn't play nice. We also used bitsandbytes sometimes for int8 matmul kernels on A100s. There was a lot of kernel selection heuristics, like picking the fused attention kernel for medium sequence lengths.
[02:05] Elaine: Also fyi, we had some KV cache issues on long chat workloads — more like our prefix caching was blowing up in memory for multi-turn sessions. We layered a tiered cache so hot prefixes stayed on-GPU and cold prefixes dropped to nvme-backed cache. That was a whole project.
[02:25] Ethan: NVMe-backed cache, ok. How did you handle the consistency between GPU cache and NVMe?
[02:29] Elaine: We used per-request versioning and a simple LRU with async writeback. It meant more engineering but helped with throughput stabili— stability. There were a few times where the async path introduced tail-latency spikes; we mitigated with batching and backpressure.
[02:44] Samira: Good detail. Quick logistics — what's your notice period and what are you looking for next?
[02:50] Elaine: Two weeks notice ideally, because I'm contracting some wrap-up. I'm looking for a team that's production-focused — low tolerance for flakiness, focuses on perf/cost tradeoffs, wants to own infra. Also interested in private deployments — I worked on a few on-prem rollouts where we had to support offline KMS and air-gapped installs.
[03:12] Samira: Redwood does both hosted and private, and engineering often works across both. Salary band question — any constraints?
[03:19] Elaine: I'm in the 180–230k base band depending on the equity and role. Open to discussion.
[03:27] Ethan: Cool. Shifting to some systems design — imagine you're designing an inference service to serve a family of 2B-7B decoder-only models for a chat product with 95% short session lengths (<=128 tokens) but occasional long sessions to 2k tokens. What architecture and strategies do you pick for latency and cost?
[03:46] Elaine: Hmm. For that distribution I'd probably optimize the majority path for small sequences — choose kernels that favor short seq performance and enable auto-batching with small max batch size so tail latency stays low. Use mixed precision + int8 where safe. For the long sessions, route to a special pool with more memory and different kernels; potentially use chunked KV cache eviction so the long sessions don't steal GPU memory from short sessions. Also I'd deploy a lightweight routing layer that can do per-request policy — so high-priority or paid customers go to low-latency pool.
[04:20] Ethan: How do you handle batching for short requests without making p95 explode?
[04:24] Elaine: Adaptive batching: start with small batch windows and if load increases, grow the window. Also reserve a small portion of capacity for immediate-exec (no-batch) so spikes from interactive users don't suffer. For example, find a sweet spot via QPS vs latency curves and set autoscaler thresholds appropriately.
[04:40] Ethan: Any experience with kernel selection at runtime?
[04:43] Elaine: Yes, we implemented a simple heuristic — sequence length histograms are collected and for each model variant we maintain a preferred kernel map keyed by length ranges. At rollout time we run microbenchmarks to update the map. It worked okay though it added complexity for model variants.
[05:00] Samira: Some phonescreen fluff — what's a technical challenge you had to convince leadership to invest in?
[05:06] Elaine: Convincing them to fund NVMe-backed cache for conversational workloads. Initial ask looked expensive, but I built a cost model showing improved utilization and reduced GPU scaling events, plus latency improvements for long sessions. It switched the conversation.
[05:20] Ethan: Follow-up: how did you measure the cost savings?
[05:23] Elaine: We instrumented per-request token-level cost, included NVMe IO amortized costs, and compared autoscaler events before/after. There was a reduction in >25% in GPU-hours for the same workload shape in our staging load tests.
[05:36] Ethan: Nice. Ok, a narrow technical question — how do you store and retrieve KV cache for multi-tenant GPUs without cross-tenant leaks?
[05:44] Elaine: Namespace isolation is critical. We used per-tenant namespaces in the cache and enforced strict GPU memory partitioning. For eviction and swapping to NVMe we attach metadata tokens to each entry and validate on restore. For hardware-level isolation on shared clusters we favored soft partitioning and then moved problematic tenants to dedicated pools.
[06:06] Ethan: Have you dealt with model parallelism for larger models?
[06:09] Elaine: Less so in my recent role — we tried model sharding for 20B models but it increased complexity and led to higher tail latencies, so we pushed those to dedicated instances. My sweet spot is 2B–8B where single-GPU inference with quantization is performant.
[06:27] Elaine: Also I built a small tooling piece that auto-detects receptive field and suggests chunked attention kernels for streaming outputs, that helped with throughput for streaming chat.
[06:37] Ethan: You mentioned tooling — what are you most comfortable writing: Python, Go, Rust?
[06:41] Elaine: Python for orchestration and tooling, a fair bit of C++ for kernels, and a little Rust for some NVMe components. I'm open to learning more Go.
[06:50] Samira: Behavioral fit — how do you prefer to work with product and SRE?
[06:54] Elaine: I like close collaboration with product on SLOs and feature scoping, and with SRE on runbooks and escalations. In previous teams we did monthly joint postmortems and it helped cleanly split ownership.
[07:03] Samira: Anything in your past that would make you a stretch for the role?
[07:07] Elaine: Maybe my lack of experience with extremely large models (>>20B) but I'm strong in the operational patterns and can ramp.
[07:15] Ethan: Two quick scenario checks — 1) a retail customer reports p99 spikes after a deploy, what instrumentation do you look at first? 2) A slow drift in recall post-quantization, what would you do?
[07:25] Elaine: 1) check tail-latency histograms by region, recent autoscaler events, any NVMe IO queue depth spikes, and recent kernel changes; also validate traffic routing policies. 2) run A/B with float baseline, look at per-layer activation distributions, try per-channel calibration or small QAT for the drifting layers.
[07:47] Ethan: Good answers.
[07:50] -- small pause while we check notes --
[08:00] Samira: Ok Elaine, want to ask us anything about the role or Redwood?
[08:05] Elaine: Yeah — curious about how much ownership infra engineers get for the private deployment work vs those are handled by a separate ops team? Also curious about the expected on-call cadence.
[08:16] Ethan: We split ownership: infra engineers are expected to own core runtime components and play a big role in private deployments alongside a deployment engineering team that helps with packaging and on-site logistics. On-call is shared, usually 1:8 or 1:10 depending on team size, but we try to reduce pager noise with good automation.
[08:36] Elaine: That sounds reasonable. Does Redwood encourage experimental quant profiles in prod?
[08:41] Ethan: We have a canary and rollout system; you can propose quant profiles, run evals against prompt sets and gated rollouts. There's also tooling to detect regressions versus golden prompts.
[08:53] Elaine: Nice.
[08:55] Samira: Last few mins — any red flags or concerns from you?
[08:59] Elaine: Not really; just want to ensure the role allows hands-on infra work and opportunities to drive perf improvements.
[09:06] Samira: Great. We'll wrap — thanks for your time. We'll share notes with the panel and come back about next steps.
[09:14] Elaine: Awesome, thanks.

[09:16] End call.
